item.title: JCI Dhaka Astral's Capitalizer 2026 concludes
item.description:
By FE YOUTH DESK

The Grand Finale of JCI Dhaka Astral Presents Capitalizer 2026, powered by Eastern Bank PLC and ACI Limited, and co-powered by Gold Kinen, concluded successfully at Radisson Blu Dhaka recently. The flagship competition, organised by BUP Finance Society under the Department of Business Administration in Finance and Banking at Bangladesh University of Professionals, brought together some of the country's most promising talents in financial strategy and investment thinking from universities across the country.

More than 300 teams from over 30 universities participated in the competition. Following two intense preliminary rounds, six finalist teams advanced to the Grand Finale. At every stage, teams were evaluated on the depth of their financial ideas and how thoughtfully they demonstrated the ability to navigate uncertainty and complex business situations.

The event witnessed a fiercely contested final showdown in which Assets = Capital + Liabilities from BUP emerged as Champion of Capitalizer 2026, distinguishing themselves through confidence and exceptional command of ideas on a highly demanding stage. Team 505 from the University of Dhaka and Team The Godfathers, also from BUP, were named first and second runners-up respectively, each bringing analytical depth and composure that made the finale as competitive as it was compelling.

Major General ASM Ridwanur Rahman, director general of the Bangladesh Institute of International and Strategic Studies (BIISS), attended the event as the chief guest.

Brigadier General Md Aminul Akbar Khan, dean of the Faculty of Business Studies at Bangladesh University of Professionals, and Lieutenant Colonel Md Atique Chowdhury, chairman of the Department of Business Administration in Finance and Banking of BUP were also present. Their presence underscored the university's continued support for student-led initiatives and its commitment to academic development. The event also welcomed representatives from partner organisations and leading corporate institutions, reflecting the growing collaboration between academia and the corporate sector.

The judging panel comprised respected academics, finance professionals, and corporate leaders who evaluated the finalist teams on strategic clarity, financial insight, and presentation quality.

As Capitalizer 2026 drew to a close, the competition reaffirmed its standing as the platform against which serious financial minds in this country measure themselves. For every team that took the stage and was tested at that level, the experience is one they will carry forward long after the night has passed.

item.title: A solution towards future unemployment problem of Bangladesh
item.description:
By TASNIMUL ISLAM

A quiet revolution is taking place in a nation where almost one in three recent graduates find it difficult to secure official work. Bangladesh is becoming a worldwide leader in digital and platform-based labour as millions of young people avoid traditional employment lines and forge their own pathways in the gig economy. The gig economy has developed from a "side hustle" into a vital safety net, swallowing a generation at risk of unemployment, from freelancers in isolated villages coding for Silicon Valley to delivery riders navigating Dhaka's crowded streets.

A convincing picture of this change is shown by recent statistics. The Social Security Policy Support (SSPS) Programme estimates that Bangladesh's freelance business alone is already worth US$ 500 million a year, with a clear trend towards a US$1.0 billion industry by 2030. With 16 per cent of the worldwide market, the nation is the second-largest supplier of online labour in the world, only surpassed by India. Even more significantly, the youth of the nation are driving this economic engine. A "Youth Revolution" in the industry is shown by a demographic analysis: an astounding 78 per cent of freelancers are between the ages of 18 and 30. Additionally, a startling 80.8 per cent of these gig workers have postsecondary degrees, suggesting that freelancing has developed into a professional outlet for recent college graduates who are unable to obtain employment in the public or traditional corporate sectors. The number of contract workers, which encompasses ride-sharing drivers, delivery couriers, and e-commerce entrepreneurs, has surpassed one million. Some estimates suggest that the figure is closer to 1.5 million when informal sector workers are included.

The government is aggressively attempting to mainstream gig labour as a remedy for unemployment after realising its potential. A large-scale training programme for freelancers is presently being carried out in 48 districts by the Ministry of Youth and Sports.These activities have quantifiable outcomes. According to ministry data, as many as 10,800 young people had finished training under this initiative as of December 2025. Remarkably, 6,732 trainees, or more than 62 per cent of those trained, have successfully begun making money in both local and foreign markets, bringing in close to US$ 1.14 million thus far. Dr Asif Nazrul called for the programme to go from teaching 18,000 young people to eventually reaching 1.8 million, emphasising that it is only getting started. The gig economy has structural issues despite its success, especially with relation to gender participation. Due to social safety concerns and what experts refer to as the "Maternal Wall," women barely make up 9.0 per cent to 10 per cent of the freelance sector. But the e-commerce industry is undergoing a revolutionary change. According to a 2022 Meta study, 70 per cent of Facebook-based companies founded since the epidemic are owned by women, and groups like the "Women and e-Commerce Forum" have more than a million members.

On January 13, 2026, the government introduced the National Freelancer Registration and ID Card Management Platform in order to resolve vulnerabilities and legitimise the industry. Due to a lack of official job credentials, freelancers were previously unable to receive credit card services, loans, or formal banking thanks to this free ID card. Additionally, in a historic step this month, the government passed an ordinance modifying the Labour Act to recognise the rights of digital platform-based workers in the official sector and provide them with legal protection for the first time. Experts caution about the "dark side" of the gig economy, which is marked by a lack of social safety nets and unstable revenue, despite the fact that it gives freedom and income. Nearly half of Bangladeshi freelancers make less than US$ 208 a month, according to research, underscoring the disparity between involvement and affluence. However, the gig economy is expected to contribute up to 2.0 per cent of Bangladesh's GDP (gross domestic product) by 2026, with internet penetration reaching 77 per cent and mobile finance services like bKash bridging the gap to the official sector. The gig economy seems to be more than a band-aid solution to the nation's high unemployment rates. The digital safety net created by and for young people is quickly becoming an indispensable part of the job market.

Despite its impressive expansion, the gig economy remains structurally unstable, built on a system that puts its employees at risk both financially and legally. The most urgent problem is the lack of official legal recognition. Gig workers are stuck in a "legal limbo" where they are neither fully protected as independent contractors nor acknowledged as employees, due to labour laws that were written before the emergence of digital platforms. The International Labour Organization believes that misclassifying workers as independent contractors lowers labour expenses by 25-30 per cent at the expense of workers, by allowing platforms to evade obligations for minimum wage, sick leave, and social security. Severe infrastructure flaws, such as frequent power outages and internet blackouts that are frequently worse outside of Dhaka, (With median fixed broadband speeds of 50-60 Mbps and mobile speeds sometimes dipping below 20 Mbps, internet quality in Bangladesh is increasing but is still below the worldwide average; poor international routing and excessive latency impede overall quality) exacerbate this lack of safety by interfering with workflows, causing freelancers to miss deadlines, and harming Bangladesh's standing as a trustworthy outsourcing location. Additionally, the industry faces pervasive gender-specific barriers; women make up only 10 per cent of the freelance workforce. These barriers range from widespread cyber-harassment and the lack of high-quality daycare facilities to societal pressure to manage household responsibilities and a lack of family support. Lastly, even for those who overcome these obstacles, the work itself is characterised by precarity and market saturation, marked by erratic, algorithm-driven wages, a dearth of social safety nets like health insurance or pensions, and an increasingly crowded market where the emergence of AI tools threatens to devalue entry-level employment.

To turn the gig economy from a shaky safety net into a long-term and respectable source of employment, it is imperative to address these fundamental problems. The 2.7 million jobless people and the more than 700,000 fresh graduates entering the workforce annually will have a flexible entry point if calculated steps are taken by our government.

Dr Tasnimul Islam is assistant professor and head of Center for Research and Development (CRD) at Army Institute of Business Administration, Sylhet (Army-IBA).

item.title: Why Bangladesh must build its brand before the world builds one for it
item.description:
By Hisham Khan AND Tanjim Hasan Chowdhury

When a business owner in California types "hire virtual assistant" into a search engine, the results are not random. They are the product of years of deliberate positioning, cultural fluency in the global market, and a country that decided its workers would not merely compete but would come to define an entire category of professional service. That country is the Philippines, and the lesson it holds for Bangladesh is one that no training programme alone can deliver.

Freelancing is no longer solely about skill, because at a certain point the market stops evaluating individuals and starts evaluating countries, and that shift rewards reputation far more than it rewards competence alone.

The brand Bangladesh has not built: Bangladesh occupies a genuinely strong position but mostly on paper. With approximately 650,000 registered freelancers and a market share estimated at 16 per cent of global online labour supply, the country is the second-largest supplier of freelance services in the world. The names and faces that global clients associate with remote work, however, are rarely Bangladeshi. The country exports talent in enormous quantities while exporting almost no narrative about that talent.

"I have clients in Germany and the UK who were genuinely surprised to learn I was from Bangladesh," says Sabbir Hossain, a Dhaka-basedfreelancer who has worked remotely for global agencies and professionals as their virtual assistant. "They assumed I was from the Philippines or India. That is not an insult. It just shows how little the world knows about us despite what we produce."That gap between output and perception is precisely where country branding operates.

Case study—what the Philippines built, and how: Over the past two decades, the Philippines did not merely enter the global services market. It claimed a corner of it so thoroughly that the phrase "virtual assistant" has become functionally synonymous with Filipino professionals in the minds of Western clients and business owners, and none of that happened by chance.

The Philippine government, working in close alignment with industry bodies such as the IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines (IBPAP), invested in a coherent national narrative: Filipino professionals are communicative, culturally attuned to Western norms, proficient in English, and dependable. That narrative was reinforced through export data, community visibility, and a generation of freelancers who presented themselves collectively rather than as isolated individuals.

Filipino professionals cultivated a reputation for warmth and reliability that became one of the most commercially valuable soft-skill brands in the global services industry. Their communication style, characteristically patient, respectful, and measured even under pressure, translated well across cultures that prize approachability in client-facing roles. A strong command of English, shaped in part by the country's history with American education systems and an entertainment culture saturated with Western media, meant that Filipino workers could handle client correspondence with care, conduct calls without friction, and produce content that required minimal revision. The quality of those interactions lodged itself in client memory, and word spread through the small-business networks and entrepreneur communities of the English-speaking world in the way that reliable service always spreads: quietly, persistently, and faster than any marketing campaign.

What accumulated over time was more durable than goodwill. Filipino agencies today do not simply supply remote workers to clients in the United States and Europe but sit at the other side of the hiring table altogether. Platforms such as Virtual Staff Finder, OnlineJobs.ph, and Remote Staff operate as intermediaries who package Filipino labour for foreign markets, building their own commercial standing on top of a national reputation. A business owner in London seeking a customer service team does not search for candidates one by one but approaches platforms that already carry the trust the Philippines built over two decades.

The scale of what that trust built is visible in the revenue figures. The Philippines' IT and business process management sector generated approximately 32.5 billion US dollars in 2022, employing more than 1.5 million workers, with industry projections placing the total above 59 billion dollars by 2028. Remote freelancing and virtual assistance form a growing share of that figure, channelling foreign exchange directly into household incomes across provinces far removed from Manila. Country branding, understood in this light, is not a cultural indulgence but a long-term economic investment with returns that the Philippines has already collected.

"When a client asks where I am from, I still notice a small hesitation when I say Bangladesh," says Nusrat Jahan, a content writer who has been working with Australian and Canadian clients since 2021. "Filipino freelancers don't face that. They already have a reputation. We have to earn trust individually every single time, and that is exhausting," she adds.That exhaustion is not a personal failing but a structural cost that falls on individual workers precisely because no institution has been built to shoulder it at a national level.

Brand is now an infrastructure: Policymakers sometimes treat country branding as a communications exercise: a logo, a tagline, a presence at international trade expos. The Philippine model demands something far more rigorous. Brand, in the freelancing context, is built through consistent quality signals over time, through sector specialisation, through professional communities that are visible internationally, and through regulatory frameworks that give clients abroad confidence in the people they are hiring.

Bangladesh launched its National Freelancer ID Card in January 2026, a meaningful first step toward formal institutional recognition. Labour Act amendments passed the same month extended legal protections to platform-based workers for the first time in the country's history. These are the foundations on which a credible brand can be constructed. The question is whether the government treats them as ends in themselves or as the opening chapter of a longer and more deliberate positioning effort.

"The ID card matters, but clients abroad don't know it exists," says Rafiqul Islam, who runs a small digital agency in Chattogram that sources contracts from UK-based businesses. "For country branding to work, it has to be visible to the people doing the hiring, not just to us."

What Rafiqul describes points to the missing actor in Bangladesh's freelancing story: the private sector institution willing to carry the national brand as part of its commercial mission.

The lesson from Sony: When Akio Morita co-founded Sony in post-war Japan, the country's manufacturing reputation in Western markets was poor. "Made in Japan" was a phrase associated with inexpensive imitation goods rather than precision engineering. Morita understood that Sony's commercial future depended on rehabilitating that association, and he pursued it with the same discipline he applied to product design. Sony did not merely sell transistor radios but sold the idea that Japan made things of quality, and it did so consistently, visibly, and over decades, until the world accepted that proposition as obvious.

From supplier to authority: The Philippines did not brand itself broadly but it chose sectors, principally business process outsourcing, virtual assistance, and customer support, and drove depth in those areas until Filipino professionals became the default association in the minds of hiring managers worldwide. Bangladesh has well-established strengths in software development, graphic design, and digital marketing that could anchor a comparable sectoral identity. The country also has a diaspora spread across the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, and the Gulf states, communities that could carry a story about Bangladeshi professional quality into markets where it has not taken hold.

Bangladesh already has the workforce to be taken seriously; what it has not built is the institutional and commercial architecture that would make the rest of the world take it seriously without being told to.

item.title: The Journey of Farhan Ahmed Prottoy: Creativity, entrepreneurship and digital growth
item.description:
By FE Online

Farhan Ahmed Prottoy, widely known as Farhan, has established himself as a prominent Bangladeshi content creator and entrepreneur. Through music videos, dramas, and digital content, he has built a strong presence across social media. Rather than identifying himself solely as a content creator, Farhan says he prefers to be recognised as an entrepreneur because entrepreneurship creates opportunities beyond personal success.

Born and raised in Cumilla, Farhan began his journey as a blogger and TikToker before entering the media industry at the age of 18. His first major breakthrough came with the music video How Funny, which introduced him to a wider audience. One of his most recognised works, Rupoboti Ek Meyer Preme Porechi, has surpassed37 million views on YouTube. Over the years, he has also appeared in more than ten music videos and over five television dramas.

Reflecting on his journey, Farhan says his passion for being in front of the camera started in childhood, but turning that dream into reality required years of dedication and persistence. He recalls creating videos with limited equipment during his early days and gradually improving his work through continuous learning and hard work. According to him, buying his first iPhone marked a turning point, enabling him to produce better quality content and connect with a much larger audience.

Farhan believes that every project is an opportunity to challenge himself, explore new ideas, and offer something meaningful to his followers. He credits the continued love and support of his audience as one of the biggest reasons behind his success and says he remains grateful for their constant encouragement.

Outside the entertainment industry, Farhan and his wife have built Samba Elite Beauty Lounge in Kandirpar, Cumilla, which he describes as a shared dream reflecting their commitment to entrepreneurship. Looking ahead, Farhan says he aims to continue creating meaningful content while expanding his business ventures and contributing to new employment opportunities.

item.title: Inside our growing pet culture
item.description:
By Mumtahina Rahman Tajree

Moomtahina Mehnaz Aniva did not plan for five kittens. She just adopted Mithi, a desi cat, because she loved animals and thought a pet would make the apartment feel more alive. Mithi had other ideas. Five kittens later, Aniva and her family spent weeks finding each one a loving home through adoption. Then came Ori, a seven-month-old Persian, calm and affectionate where Mithi is restless. Then the budgerigars. Then the aquarium. "Having all of them around makes our home feel much happier," she says. "The cats are especially attached to my mother, who takes care of almost everything for them."

Dhaka was never a pet city. It is becoming one anyway, apartment by apartment, one adoption at a time. In small flats and family homes, among students living alone and households that swore they would only get one, the same thing keeps happening. The animals stay. The attachment grows. And an economy nobody quite planned for has built itself around both.

The numbers behind the affection

When DUCSU organised Dhaka University's first Pet Carnival at TSC in collaboration with the Ministry of Fisheries and Livestock and Care DU, it was not just an event. It was a signal that pet culture had moved beyond individual households and into public cultural space, mainstream enough to warrant a university-level celebration.

According to research by Mohammad Abdul Saleque of ACI Limited, pet owners in Bangladesh have increased by 170 per cent over the last three years, with 90 per cent of those pets being cats.

The industry is estimated at over BDT 230 crore annually and is growing 10 to 15 per cent per year.

The cat food market alone is valued at BDT 5 billion, with BDT 4 billion met through imports primarily from China, Thailand, and Turkey.

The Department of Livestock recorded 32,156 tonnes of cat food imported in 2024-25.

Pet supplies are now available in over 4,000 pet shops across the country, where they were once confined to a handful of import sections in upscale supermarkets.

Nuclear families, rising rates of people living alone, and pandemic-era isolation have all pushed people toward animals as companions.

Social media accelerated the shift considerably, with Facebook communities like Cat Lovers BD, Dog Lovers Society, and Bangladesh Lovebird Society becoming active hubs for adoption, advice, and community.

Cats dominate because Dhaka's apartments demand it. Dogs need space and outdoor access that most flats cannot offer, making miniature breeds the practical choice for those determined to keep one.

Why people are choosing pets

The motivations vary, but their emotional core is consistent.

Mollika Mukherjee got River, her Japanese Spitz, on her therapist's recommendation during a severe depressive episode.

Living alone in a one-bedroom apartment, a miniature breed was the most practical option. "Dogs are incredibly loyal and are the perfect companions anyone could ask for," she says. "I am much happier than I was before."

Mahmuda Rahman, a travel agency owner, took a completely different route. She saw Shirooo on Facebook, fell in love, and brought her home the same week with no prior plan.

When she comes home after a long day, Shirooo jumps into her arms. "I think she is a member of my house, so she should be cared for just like the other members."

Sharmin Alam, who runs a homemade food business in Dhanmondi, keeps a myna and a quail and spends BDT 2,000 to 3,000 monthly on quality feed, supplements, and toys. The birds, she says, have given her daily routine a rhythm and her stress levels a reason to drop.

Mim, a student split between Dhaka and its outskirts, has five rescued and adopted deshi cats. "I would rather spend my money giving one of them a home than buy a foreign breed," she says.

Tahsin Jahan Siddika, living alone in Dhaka, bought budgerigars during the pandemic out of loneliness, including one disabled bird nobody else would take. When university forced her to leave them behind, they did not survive. "Due to lack of care, they eventually died." The sentence carries more weight than she gives it.

Veterinary professionals in Dhaka who have watched the shift from across the consultation table point to a consistent pattern.

People dealing with loneliness, mental health struggles, and the isolation of urban life are increasingly turning to pets to fill a gap that human connection has not been able to.

What it actually costs

Mollika's monthly costs stay under BDT 1,000, though vaccinations recently ran BDT 2,800.

Mim's five cats cost BDT 1,500 to 2,000 monthly. Mahmuda spends around BDT 4,000 on Shirooo, plus BDT 4,500 for home grooming sessions. Aniva's household spends around BDT 5,000 across all pets, with neutering and spaying recently adding BDT 8,000.

Private clinic consultations cost around BDT 600. Core vaccines run BDT 200 to 1,500. Neutering costs BDT 1,000 to 3,000; spaying BDT 1,500 to 4,000. Grooming sessions run BDT 2,000 to 5,000.

Government hospitals offer vaccinations at lower prices but do not typically perform surgical procedures on cats.

Bangladesh now has over 225 private pet clinics, most recently established and concentrated in Dhaka's wealthier neighbourhoods.

The industry's darker side

The growth of pet culture has not been matched by proportional growth in welfare standards. Sellers without licensing remain widespread. Markets like Katabon in Dhaka, where Mollika purchased River, have been flagged by animal welfare groups for keeping animals in cramped, inhumane conditions and trading in stolen animals.

Legitimate boarding facilities are rare and overwhelmed. Daily rates range from BDT 400 to BDT 2,500, yet during Eid-ul-Fitr one Gulshan facility turned away around 40 customers from a single branch despite being fully booked. For most pet owners, reliable boarding does not exist.

Many leave pets with neighbours or domestic help, with unpredictable results. Siddika's birds did not survive such an arrangement.

Mollika raises another gap few discuss openly: public transport in Dhaka is almost entirely pet-unfriendly.

The legal framework governing all of this is alarmingly thin. Bangladesh's Cruelty to Animals Act dates to 1920, with fines as low as BDT 100.

A new Animal Welfare Act has been cabinet-approved but not gazetted. Pet sellers face no licensing requirement, breeders face no welfare standards, and the sector has no regulatory oversight. Recent commentary from local media and animal welfare advocates has called for modernising Bangladesh's pet laws. At the same time, Bangladesh continues to operate under a colonial-era framework.

What the culture is really about

Aniva's cats greet her when she comes home. Sharmin's birds have changed her mornings. Mahmuda's Shirooo jumps into her arms at the end of every long day. Mollika is measurably happier than she was before River.

People needed something to come home to. In Dhaka, they found it. The economy will keep growing, and the welfare gaps will need addressing, but neither of those things is why it started. Nor is it why it will continue.

item.title: Why protecting Gen Alpha and Z online can no longer wait
item.description:
By SAIMA NUR

Think back to childhood in the 1990s. Evenings meant cousins from both sides of the family gathered in one courtyard. Grandparents told stories after dinner. Neighbours' children ran in and out of homes without knocking. Games needed no batteries. Friendships needed no wifi.

A child's world was full of real faces, real voices, and real touch.

That world has quietly disappeared for many children today. A phone now fills the space once filled by an uncle's teasing or a grandmother's lap. Screens have replaced courtyards. Likes have replaced laughter. This shift has come at a cost, and Bangladeshi parents need to understand what that cost is.

The hidden harm

A child glued to a screen is not simply distracted. Their brain is still developing, and constant screen exposure shapes it in ways researchers are still uncovering.

Attention spans shrink. Sleep suffers. Emotional regulation weakens. Children start to prefer a glowing screen over a warm hug, because the screen asks nothing of them and gives instant reward in return.

There is also a darker layer to this. The internet is not a childproofed space. Predators, harmful content, and exploitative apps exist alongside educational videos and cartoons.

A child left alone with a device faces risks that no previous generation faced.

Shishurai Shob, a Bangladeshi child protection initiative, has repeatedly flagged this concern. Their research notes that Bangladeshi parents themselves need to reduce their own screen time, especially when children are around, as part of protecting children from screen addiction.

Their work also stresses that countless children in Bangladesh are now spending excessive time on screens, which harms not just their eyesight but their overall development, a trend they describe as alarming.

What children actually need

A child does not need more apps. A child needs more people. An uncle who wrestles with him in the yard teaches him about boundaries and physical trust.

A grandmother who braids her hair while telling old stories teaches patience and heritage. Cousins who fight over a bicycle teach negotiation. A screen can replicate none of this, however well designed.

This is not a call to remove technology from a child's life. Devices are part of modern learning and modern life. The call is for balance. A child's day should include real people before it includes a device. Study time should be guided by a parent sitting nearby, not by a tablet propped in a corner.

What parents can do

Parents can start with small, practical steps. Set fixed hours for screen use, and keep those hours away from meals and bedtime.

Encourage weekend visits to grandparents and extended family, even when it feels inconvenient.

Sit with children during their study time rather than handing them a device and walking away. Ask children what they watch, and watch some of it together.

Parents' and teachers' responsibility begins at the start. That awareness must spread through communities, since a child's protection cannot rest on any one person alone.

Bangladeshi childhood once meant a house full of people. It can mean that again. The choice sits with today's parents.
item.author: SAIMA NUR

item.title: Musical instruments you can learn after 30
item.description:
By Prokash Sikder

You return home from a long day at the office. Your brain feels completely fried. You immediately reach for your phone and start scrolling through social media out of pure exhaustion. This is the modern adult trap.

We constantly seek passive entertainment to forget our daily stress. But there is a much better way to reset your brain. Picking up a musical instrument as an adult is the ultimate stress hack. Many people believe you cannot learn music after childhood, but your brain can learn new skills at any age.

The science of musical healing

Playing an instrument actively changes your brain chemistry. It is not just a simple distraction.

A 2021 study published in the International Journal of Music, Health and Wellbeing showed very clear results. The researchers found that playing a musical instrument significantly lowers cortisol levels. Cortisol is the body's primary stress hormone. When you focus on a melody, your brain completely stops worrying about office emails. So, in your 30s, when you're dealing with everyday stress, music can work as therapy.

Choosing the right instrument

You do not need to buy a massive drum set to start. Pick something practical for apartment living. The acoustic guitar is a classic, popular choice that you can easily practice quietly at home in your bedroom.

The ukulele is another brilliant option for beginners.

Mr. Shibly Mahbub shares his practical experience, saying, "Starting with the mouth organ could be very useful for breathing, and it is comparatively easy to learn." He is currently learning this instrument through a private music academy in Dhanmondi.

Where to learn and the costs

Finding a good teacher in Dhaka is easier than ever today. You can enroll in local music academies in neighbourhoods like Dhanmondi, Uttara, or Mirpur.

Dhaka University Band Society is one of them at TSC, where you can take classes. Classes cost around 2,000 to 3,000 Tk.

Bangladesh Shilpakala Academy at Segunbagicha and Chhayanaut at Dhanmondi offer foundational training in traditional and classical instruments, with nominal semester fees roughly around 3,000 to 5,000 BDT.

For Western contemporary and board-certified curricula, Sound of Music School at Dhanmondi and TuneLab at Bashundhara charge around 4,000 BDT monthly alongside a one-time admission fee of 4,000 BDT. Meanwhile, the Yamaha Art Center at Tejgaon offers specialised, corporate-backed programmes in guitar, piano, and drums, with structured beginner or advanced courses priced between 7,000 and 8,000 BDT. Hiring a private home tutor might cost between 4,000 and 6,000 Taka per month.

However, you don't need to spend much. The internet is full of high-quality learning resources. YouTube channels offer step-by-step beginner courses for absolutely free. You can also use popular smartphone apps for structured daily lessons. These interactive apps usually require a very small monthly subscription fee.

Managing your practice time

In our 30s, we complain about not having free time. But musicians don't need many hours. Consistency is far more important than duration.

Only fifteen to twenty minutes of focused practice will do the job; you can make up the time by cutting back on your scrolling.

You must also change your mindset about hobbies. We often feel guilty when we do something that does not generate money. You must separate your personal self-worth from economic productivity. This time belongs entirely to you. It is an investment in your own mental health.

Playing for pure joy

The goal isn't to become a famous professional musician or impress anyone. The primary goal is pure personal joy.

You will feel an incredible sense of pride when you finally play your favourite song perfectly. The strings' vibration will wash away your daily corporate fatigue. You will rediscover a beautiful and highly creative part of yourself. Stop finding excuses and buy that instrument today. Your future self will thank you deeply.
item.author: Prokash Sikder

item.title: Iran threatens 45 tankers with fines, confiscation in Hormuz escalation
item.description:
By REUTERS

Iran said it had blacklisted 45 tankers that had broken its rules for crossing the Strait of Hormuz, and would take action against any vessels transferring loads with them, escalating its threats over the key waterway six months into the war.

The named vessels could be fined, detained and have their cargoes confiscated, according to an X post late on Sunday from the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, a new body set up by Iran to manage the strait.

The warning was issued within days of the US threatening Iran with "the toughest sanctions in history", and Iran saying its response to any new US threats would be "devastating".

The restricted list includes very large crude carriers, liquefied natural gas and liquefied petroleum gas tankers, and clean product vessels, among others.

Some of the named ships are owned by the United Arab Emirates' ADNOC Logistics and Shipping (ADNOC L&S), ADNOC's subsidiary Navig8 Tankers, and Saudi Arabia's national shipping carrier Bahri.

Any vessels involved in ship-to-ship transfers with the named vessels could be added to the blacklist, the Iranian X post added.

The post did not spell out what it meant by Iran's rules, but Tehran has in the past said ship-owners should get its clearance to transit the strait and said ships should pay for security and other services.

The US has also imposed a naval blockade against Iran-related shipping.

The Gulf supplied about 20 percent of the world's daily crude oil and liquefied natural gas before the Iran conflict disrupted tanker traffic.

US-coordinated efforts to shuttle tankers quietly through the Strait of Hormuz to fill supertankers waiting just outside it are helping restore some of those export volumes.

US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said on X on Friday that the "7-day average of oil leaving the Strait is over 8 million barrels a day. Make no mistake, thanks to the US Navy, oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz."

Ships owned by Klaveness Ship Management, Stolt Tankers and South Korea's Sinokor were also included on the blacklist.

The shipping firms did not immediately respond to Reuters' requests for comment.

The Persian Gulf Strait Authority has said cargo owners should refer to an updated list of vessels deemed non-compliant for voyages relating to the Gulf.

Ships seeking the removal of their names from the non-compliant vessels' list must submit a request with relevant explanations to Iran's maritime authorities, the post said.

item.title: World misses leaders who could help restore order
item.description:
By Nilratan Halder

It could be hubris, a joke or a show of comedy had its snowballing impacts not caused bleeding to global economy, particularly those of countries like Bangladesh. The latest practical joke played by master prankster President Donald Trump is the declaration of the Hormuz Strait a US territory. Trump posted a map of the strait circling the waterway on Truth Social to indicate that it is a "new US territory". A little earlier, he threatened to bomb Oman if it "gets in the way" of a deal with Iran on Hormuz Strait. This was in reference to the ongoing talks between Oman and Iran on control of the strait. 

Here is an American president who has been talking nonsense and acting theatrically ever since his coming to power for the second time. His antics have no end. The prank master wanted to purchase Greenland and was rebuffed. Even his imposition of reciprocal tariff was declared illegal by the US Court of Appeals. The court ruled that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) does not grant the executive branch the authority to impose taxes or tariffs. That power exclusively belongs to the Congress. Now the US Treasury has been refunding the duties collected illegally to businesses. By mid-summer, the payouts have surpassed $100 billion. Bangladesh has a legitimate demand for refund of the duties on its export to that country.

However, the US president's caprice surpassed all limits when he sent troops to Venezuelan capital Caracas to capture Nicolas Maduro and his wife and intern the couple in US prison. The charge of drug smuggling is an excuse. It is a blatant violation of international laws and the United Nations charter. But who cares? Trump does not care a fig for the UN and had established instead an alternative to it called "Board of Peace" in January 2026. His megalomania has thus caused grave harm to the international political and economic order. He needed to be reined in but the execution of the most pernicious plan of controlling the petroleum business in Venezuela emboldened him to repeat a similar feat in Iran forgetful of the reality that Iran is not Venezuela.

Yet the killings of Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, cleric and supreme leader of Iran, and some top military generals by precision attacks smack of blatant violation of all international rules and laws. His calculation was to incite violent domestic opposition to the Iranian Islamic theocracy and install a puppet government in its place. But the killing of the Ayatollah only cemented the Iranian national unity and helped it delve deep into its defensive resources and resilience. Once again, Trump has met a reversal here. He may not admit this but his effort to get out of Iran faux pas, his own creation, with some semblance of dignity is quite clear.

Thus the Trump administration has been suffering setbacks one after another and such snubs neither embarrass nor perturb him. His monumental folly led him to partner with Benjamin Netanyahu in attacking Iran. The man who bragged over his power to bring an end to the Russia-Ukraine war within 24 hours has himself unleashed a war on Iran raising the spectre of a conflagration far beyond Iranian and Israeli borders. 

In an effort to bring Iran to its knees, Trump has become the architect of leading the world into an unprecedented turmoil in modern times. He is responsible for the economic bleeding nations the world over are experiencing now. Bangladesh is no exception to this rule. Many countries like Bangladesh are staring in the face of stagflation due to severe energy crises and fall in industrial production. 

If the armed conflict in the Middle East escalates to disrupt peace, the economic fallouts from it are proving no less damaging and destructive. Now Iran is dictating the terms and Trump is issuing empty threats as if to justify his aggressive role in the Israel-Iran conflict. Meanwhile, this war has relegated the genocide committed by Israel in Gaza and illegal occupation in West Bank to the back burner. The killings in Gaza and Ukraine and lately in Russia have become routine with no accountability on anyone's part. Is human life so cheap? The rest of the world stands a bystander to witness such crimes against humanity without any serious effort to stop the senseless acts of extermination. 

Such acts should have been considered an affront to and crime against civilisation but instead streaks of insanity now dominate, leaving rationality and values a casualty. If power wielders fail to realise they are behaving childishly and are determined to get their way, the world moves towards manmade catastrophes. It happened before the two World Wars. Is humanity rushing to a predicted apocalypse? A war of global proportion can destroy this planet many times over because nations have stockpiles of arsenals the most powerful bombs used by the US on two Japanese cities during the World War II could match only a fraction of their destructive power. 

Sanity seems to have taken leave of leaders of what is called the free world. Trump excels in the vicious art of pushing the world towards an ominous prospect. Nation after nation will be left with their economic backbone broken if the military and diplomatic stalemates in the Middle East continue. Disruption of the world order of coexistence, built painstakingly under UN mentoring, has brought the world to the precipice courtesy of cynical and senseless acts by Trump. Life is no longer normal. Leaders have let their peoples down. It is time for the common people across the world to raise their voices in unison against the insane and dangerous policies of 'might is right' pursued by powerful but reckless leaders like Donald Trump.
item.author: Nilratan Halder

item.title: OPPO photography contest draws 23,000 submissions
item.description:
By TECH EXPRESS DESK

OPPO's 2026 photography contest has received more than 23,000 submissions from across Bangladesh, marking a record response as the competition reaches its Grand Finale.

Organised with Pathshala South Asian Media Institute, the contest invited smartphone photographers to compete in five categories: Portrait; Nature and Wildlife; Street and Architecture; Low Light; and Heritage and Culture.

The Grand Winner will receive Tk 100,000, an OPPO flagship smartphone and a photography course. The Elite and Master winners will receive Tk 50,000 and Tk 30,000 respectively, along with smartphones and photography courses.

Each category winner will receive Tk 20,000, a smartphone and a photography course.

item.title: Khosru calls for linking higher edn to jobs
item.description:
By FE REPORT

Finance and Planning Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury on Friday called for linking higher education with employment and entrepreneurship, including meeting the demand of industries in the country.

The Finance and Planning Minister also called for taking into consideration the government's priority sectors, employment prospects and opportunities for entrepreneurship when establishing new universities and introducing new departments and subjects.

He said this during a view-sharing session with higher education policymakers on the first day of the two-day Vice-Chancellors' Dialogue organized under the Higher Education Acceleration and Transformation (HIT) project being implemented by the Bangladesh University Grants Commission (UGC).

The dialogue began at BRAC CDM in Savar.

At the same time, the ministry advised the UGC chairman not to recommend unplanned university approvals.

The exchange of views session was attended by Prime Minister's Adviser on Education, and Primary and Mass Education Mahdi Amin, National Professor Mahbub Ullah, Vice Chancellors of various public and private universities of the country, and higher education-related people.

The Minister said that the government gave the education sector top priority even amidst the economic crisis and significantly increased the budget allocation.

Stating that education also has economic value in the current market-oriented economy, he said that universities should inform industry and trade institutions about their research capabilities and innovations.

Without effective cooperation between universities and the industry, the country's research and innovation system will not be sustainable, he underlined, saying that universities should conduct research to solve the real problems of the country's industries and businesses.

At the same time, the private sector should come forward to finance university research and commercially utilise the results of research, he demanded.

Mahdi Amin said that the existing curricula of universities should be updated regularly. In addition, employment-oriented short-term courses can be introduced to improve students' communication, technology, language, problem-solving, leadership and entrepreneurship skills.

The UGC Chairman said that a significant number of young people are not getting employment opportunities even after receiving higher education.

On the one hand, employers are not getting the necessary skilled manpower; while on the other hand, highly educated youths are being deprived of job opportunities.

To reduce this gap, necessary changes should be made in the curricula, teaching methods and evaluation systems of universities. "We need to upgrade our higher education" to world standards, he added.

item.title: Accord opens avenues for tech jobs in Oman
item.description:
By FE REPORT

An accord between a Bangladeshi and an Oman-based technology firms is likely to open avenues for tech jobs in the gulf country for skilled talents, besides promoting cooperation in other economic fields. 

Bangladeshi software-firm Brain Station 23 signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Star Drones, an Oman-based technology company, to collaborate on drone technology, software engineering, and robotics.

The MoU was signed in Dhaka on Thursday, in presence of business leaders and company executives.

MJ Ferdous, Director at Brain Station 23, and Said Abdul Ghafoor Saif Udeen, Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of Star Drones, headquartered at Innovation Park Muscat in Seeb, Oman, inked the deal.

Under the MoU, Brain Station 23 will provide high-skilled engineering talent to support Star Drones' software development for agricultural and industrial applications.

The technical support will primarily be delivered remotely by Bangladeshi engineers, with provisions for on-site deployment in Oman as needed.

Speaking at the ceremony, Ashraful Haq Chowdhury, president, Saudi Arabia-Bangladesh Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SABCCI), said Bangladesh is keen to deepen its trade, investment, and manpower collaboration with Oman in line with Oman's 'Vision 2040' development agenda.

Chowdhury highlighted the deep economic ties between the two nations, pointing out that around 1.0 million Bangladeshi nationals are currently employed in Oman.

"We want to expand our skilled human resources to support Oman's ongoing infrastructure and economic development," Chowdhury said.

"At the same time, we want to see bilateral trade and investment relationships between Oman and Bangladesh grow day by day."

He points out that the Omani government's Vision 2040 framework presents significant opportunities for Bangladeshi firms and skilled workers to participate in major infrastructure and development projects across the Sultanate.

The delegation, led by Omani business leader Said, spent five "very busy days exploring potential areas of collaboration and investment in Bangladesh", Chowdhury added, expressing optimism about future joint ventures between the private sectors of both countries.

Star Drones hopes to offer hardware and software solutions as a cost-effective alternative to Chinese models, opening potential opportunities for technology imports to Bangladesh and broader regional exports.

Addressing the function, Abdul Ghafoor Saif Udeen underscored the importance of gradually strengthening bilateral cooperation through people-to-people exchanges, trade, and knowledge sharing.

He said initial collaboration in areas such as human resources, agriculture, and professional expertise could help build a stronger foundation for long-term economic ties.

Udeen also stressed the potential to expand cooperation into technology-driven sectors, including artificial intelligence, drone technology, and software development.

"Leveraging the strengths of both countries could create new opportunities for innovation, investment, and sustainable economic growth," he said.

Bassim Allah Bakhsh Ghulam Al-Zadjali, Chief Technology Officer (CTO), Star Drones, Innovation Park Muscat, Seeb, Sultanate of Oman, also was present at the event.
